description: We are a team of tech enthusiasts passionate about innovation and solving real-world challenges. Our skills span AI/ML, Python, full-stack development, data analysis, and UI/UX design. We combine technical expertise with creative problem-solving and collaborative thinking to build impactful solutions. With a shared interest in space technology, Earth observation, and emerging technologies, we aim to turn ambitious ideas into practical innovations.
summary:
AeroTerra is a web tool that searches all of Earth's ice-free land for places that can stand in for two exploration targets: the Shackleton rim at the Moon's south pole and Jezero crater on Mars. It measures the targets and 5.58 million Earth tiles the same way from open NASA data (terrain from LOLA, MOLA and SRTM, emissivity from ASTER, temperature from MODIS) and scores each physical dimension separately.

Its core idea is inspired by primal and dual problems in optimisation theory. We ask one question two ways: which place is most similar to the target, and which place needs the fewest changes to become it. For Mars both arrive at the same top site, and 86 of the 100 most similar tiles need no site-specific change.

The search masks famous analog sites, and points to candidates we found no published analog study for, including two basalt lava fields in Saudi Arabia. Every site also lists what it cannot teach, so field teams know an analog's limits before they travel.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

AeroTerra is an interactive map. You pick a target (Moon: Shackleton rim, or Mars: Jezero crater), set the search, and select a site. For each site it shows a score for every physical dimension, a checklist of the changes the place would still need to match the target, the measured values, and a list of what the site cannot teach, such as gravity, air pressure and radiation shielding.

THE IDEA: TWO QUESTIONS THAT SHOULD CONVERGE

The design is inspired by primal and dual problems in optimisation theory, where a maximisation problem is paired with a minimisation problem and both reach the same optimal value. AeroTerra asks:

- Forward (maximise similarity): which place on Earth is most similar to the target?

- Reverse (minimise changes): which place needs the fewest changes to become the target?

We then check whether the two ranked lists converge. For Mars they do: both choose the same first site, and 86 of the 100 most similar tiles need zero site-specific changes. For the Moon agreement is weaker (29 of 100). Without our thermal score in the forward question only 10 of 100 agree, which shows the reverse question catches a dimension the forward one lacks. This is an informal analogue, not a formal dual: the reverse question is defined separately and the two rankings share inputs, so we treat convergence as a consistency check.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Target statistics (mean slope, 95th-percentile slope, roughness exponent) are measured from LRO LOLA for Shackleton and MGS MOLA for Jezero.

2. The same statistics are computed for 5.58 million Earth land tiles (0.05 degrees, about 5.5 km) from SRTM30, together with ASTER GED five-band emissivity and NDVI, and MODIS day and night surface temperature.

3. Each dimension is scored on its own as a distance to the target in units of Earth's own spread. There is no combined score, so a weak dimension cannot hide.

4. A one-dimensional ground heat-conduction model is fitted to each tile's MODIS readings and re-run under the target's sky, Sun and day length. This gives a "thermal twin" score and the conversion checklist.

5. Seven famous analog regions (Iceland, Hawaii, Atacama, Haughton, Meteor Crater, Rio Tinto, Etna) are masked, and sixteen areas with published analog work are flagged.

RESULTS

- 2,834 tiles (0.05%) need no site-specific change for Mars, and 148 for the Moon.

- Candidates with no published analog study found in our web search: the Harrat Uwayrid area and Harrat Ithnayn in Saudi Arabia and Groot Karasberge in Namibia for Mars; the Qaanaaq area of north-west Greenland and Melville Island in Canada for the Moon. This was a web search, not a full literature review, so these are candidates to verify.

- No Earth site matches the targets' temperatures as it stands. The thermal twin shows why: Mars's air and Sun set its cold, and only soil and latitude can be supplied on Earth.

- Lonar Crater in India, our showcase, is measured from 30 m elevation data (rim 1.81 km across). The tool states plainly that a 5.5 km search cannot rank it.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Field and mission teams can shortlist analog sites by what each one can and cannot test, before paying for an expedition.

- The method is repeatable: a new target needs only its own terrain and thermal statistics.

- The thermal twin and a gravity test drive (the same rover on the same ground under Earth and target gravity) make the physics visible for students and the public.

CREATIVITY

- The reverse question and the convergence check described above.

- A thermal twin where you apply one change at a time and watch the day's temperature curve move.

- A pixel-art rover that drives a site's real terrain profile under both gravities.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- Honesty about limits: the Mars emissivity target is an Earth-basalt proxy, some thermal inputs are assumed, checklist thresholds are choices shown in the app, and a site off our known-site list is not proven new.

- Reproducibility: every number comes from open data, and the scripts that produce it are in the repository.

- Scale: a 5.5 km grid finds landscapes, not small features such as craters, caves or lava tubes.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, rasterio, h5py, Pillow) for the data pipeline. Next.js, React, TypeScript, deck.gl and MapLibre GL for the web app, hosted as static files on Vercel. NASA GIBS provides the basemap. Code, derived data and interface text were produced with an AI assistant (Claude); this is stated in the source files, the data files and on the site.

Live site: https://aeroterra-pink.vercel.app

Source: https://github.com/termuxuser123/aeroterra
